summary: CDAS proposes a coherent alternative to Lang./PO steering by combining a JSD distribution-matching objective with distributed interchange interventions, motivated by causal localization ideas. The safety case studies (refusal override and CoT backdoor neutralization) are the strongest evidence and show useful utility/KL preservation relative to RePS, but AXBENCH results are mixed and often require aggressive factor tuning that undercuts the paper’s ‘faithful / natural-factor’ narrative. Missing component ablations and limited statistical testing leave the central claim—that weaker, model-derived supervision yields more faithful bi-directional control—insufficiently established for a clear ICLR accept.
strengths: Clear problem framing that connects intervention-based steering to mechanistic/causal localization and motivates a weaker, full-vocabulary supervision signal rather than token NLL or preference ranking.
Method is concrete and implementable: contrastive DII protocol, explicit JSD objective for both elicitation and suppression, and a principled (if empirically fragile) unit-factor inference recipe.
Evaluation spans a broad concept benchmark (AXBENCH / CONCEPT500) plus two non-trivial safety suppression settings, including models up to 70B and a challenging unknown-trigger backdoor threat model.
Calibration is relatively honest: the paper reports when CDAS loses to RePS/Lang., acknowledges layer sensitivity and data requirements, and states limitations rather than claiming universal SOTA.

key_concerns.issue: The design is a compound of (i) JSD matching and (ii) DII/clamping, but there is no systematic ablation that isolates each piece under matched data, intervention family, and factor policy (e.g., JSD+addition, PO+DII, JSD with fixed vs DII-sampled factors). The ‘DAS’ baseline (Lang. objective under the CDAS protocol) is only a partial control and is confusingly named, so gains cannot be causally attributed to the proposed objective.
key_concerns.suggested_fix: Add a full 2×2 (or fuller) ablation over objective × intervention protocol, with matched training data and identical inference-time factor selection, and rename the Lang.+DII baseline to avoid implying causal-variable localization.

key_concerns.issue: The core faithfulness story (DII samples on-distribution factors; weak JSD avoids off-manifold overfitting) is weakly supported for general-purpose steering: Table 1 shows large gaps between unit-factor and tuned-factor CDAS, and RePS remains strongest in several settings. Without stronger evidence that tuned β still yields more faithful/on-distribution control than PO/Lang., the title and framing overreach the AXBENCH evidence.
key_concerns.suggested_fix: Either deliver competitive unit-factor (or lightly tuned) results, or revise claims to scope ‘faithfulness’ primarily to the suppression/utility/KL case studies and quantify off-distribution-ness (representation norms, fluency collapse, repetition) under matched strength.

key_concerns.issue: Statistical rigor is uneven: AXBENCH fair splits help, and the backdoor study reports three seeds with shaded SE, but refusal results and many benchmark deltas lack multi-seed variance, confidence intervals, or significance tests, making small/inconsistent margins hard to trust.
key_concerns.suggested_fix: Report mean±std over seeds for all main tables, fix evaluation protocols across methods, and add simple significance tests (or bootstrap CIs) for headline comparisons.

key_concerns.issue: Baseline fairness and breadth in the case studies are incomplete: BiPO is dropped for AXBENCH weakness; RePS uses tuned factors while CDAS/DAS use unit factors; DIM uses addition/ablation asymmetrically. This makes ‘CDAS is more stable/tuning-free’ partly an artifact of unequal inference budgets.
key_concerns.suggested_fix: Re-run case studies under both unit-factor and matched tuning budgets for all methods, and include at least one strong PO baseline (BiPO or RePS) under identical protocols.

key_concerns.issue: Positioning against causal abstraction is hedged in a remark that CDAS is ‘not causal variable localization,’ which is appropriate but leaves the DAS inspiration largely rhetorical without interchange-intervention success metrics or concept-isolation analyses beyond steering scores.
key_concerns.suggested_fix: Either drop strong causal-localization language in the intro/title framing, or add localization-style analyses (e.g., interchange accuracy proxies, layer-wise causal mediation, feature specificity checks).

questions_for_authors: Holding data and factor selection fixed, how much of the gain comes from JSD versus from DII/clamping alone?

Why do concept-eliciting source latents suffice as unit factors for refusal/backdoor suppression but fail for AXBENCH elicitation—does this indicate weak concept features, weak xc construction, or a mismatch between training and test strength?
Are AXBENCH and refusal improvements statistically significant across seeds/splits, and what is the variance of gpt-4o-mini / LLM-judge scores?
Under matched inference-time tuning compute, does CDAS still dominate RePS on utility/KL while remaining competitive on suppression?
How sensitive are results to the one-to-many DII source-token choice and to the gpt-generated neutral/augmented training data?
calibration_check: Claims of a more faithful, causally grounded bi-directional steering pathway are only partially scoped: the conclusion correctly admits inconsistent AXBENCH wins and factor-tuning needs, but the title/intro still oversell relative to mixed general-purpose evidence.

significance.justification: Steering/faithful control is a timely ICLR topic and the safety suppression+utility angle would interest the community, but mixed benchmark wins limit likely practice change versus RePS/Lang.

novelty.justification: JSD full-vocabulary matching for steering plus DII-based bi-directional control is a genuine combination, yet it is largely an adaptation of DAS/distillation ideas rather than a sharply new principle.

rigor.justification: The method is formally clear and experiments are thoughtful, but missing component ablations and unequal factor-tuning protocols weaken the claim–evidence link for why CDAS works.

statistical_soundness.justification: Fair AXBENCH splits and three-seed backdoor curves with SE are a start, but refusal tables and many deltas lack seeds, error bars, and significance testing.

calibration_honesty.justification: The paper reports losses to RePS/Lang., layer sensitivity, and concrete limitations; residual overclaim is mainly in the framing/title versus AXBENCH, not in hiding negatives.

clarity.justification: Overall organization and equations are followable for an expert reader, but dense extraction, the CDAS-vs-DAS naming, and several typos reduce precision.

structure_compliance.justification: Standard conference sections are present (intro, related, method, benchmark, case studies, conclusion/limitations) at a reasonable ICLR length despite anonymization artifacts.

reproducibility.justification: Data construction, objectives, intervention forms, layer choices, and factor rules are described in enough detail to reimplement in principle; anonymized links are disregarded per review rules.

related_work.justification: Steering objectives, DAS/causal localization, distribution matching, and refusal/backdoor probing are covered with a clear complementary niche, though comparison depth is limited outside the chosen baselines.

figure_quality.justification: Captions indicate informative comparative tables and layer-wise ASR plots with error shading that directly support the main empirical claims rather than decorate them.

breadth_generality.justification: CONCEPT500 breadth and multi-model safety studies help, but inconsistent layer/model wins, Gemma-centric general steering, and incomplete matched baselines undercut claimed generality.

overall_recommendation.justification: Promising complementary steering method with useful safety evidence, but blocking ablations and a partially unsupported faithfulness narrative place it at borderline-reject for ICLR 2026 as submitted.
